title: Fictional repair-shop handoff pilot
provenance: All people, statements and scenarios below are synthetic benchmark fixtures, not customer evidence.

analysis.decisionQuestion: What should a small repair-shop handoff pilot solve, which preferences genuinely conflict, and what remains unverified?
questions: Which recurring needs are supported across these selected fictional interviews? Distinguish synthesis from merely repeating quotations.
Which preferences genuinely conflict, and which can coexist? Explain the source-backed distinction without inventing a conflict.
What decision-critical evidence is missing, and what should be tested before committing to requirements?

turns.speaker: mara
turns.text: I copy the same repair status from the technician chat into our customer email, and sometimes send yesterday's status. I want one current status and one named owner for each repair.

turns.speaker: mara
turns.text: Keep customer email. I do not want us copying updates manually. For every job, assigning a technician must require the dispatcher to approve it first, even when a technician is free.

turns.speaker: mara
turns.text: We have not measured minutes spent copying. I do not know what a new tool should cost.

turns.speaker: ivo
turns.text: A job sometimes has two owners while another has none. A shared queue should show the current repair status and the single person responsible.

turns.speaker: ivo
turns.text: For every job, assign the next free technician automatically without asking the dispatcher first. A dispatcher should only correct the assignment afterwards. Customer email can stay; it is the copying I dislike.

turns.speaker: ivo
turns.text: Our workshop Wi-Fi sometimes drops, but I have not counted the outages or tested a disconnected workflow.

turns.speaker: lena
turns.text: I need to see stale repairs and who owns each one before promising a collection date. Today the queue and emails disagree about the latest status.

turns.speaker: lena
turns.text: A desktop-only pilot at our front desk is fine. I still want a shared queue; desktop-only does not mean one person's private list.

turns.speaker: lena
turns.text: We can offer one shop and two weeks for a pilot. I have not approved a budget or any customer-satisfaction target, and no customers were interviewed here.

turns.speaker: oleg
turns.text: At shift change I cannot tell whether the owner field is current. A time-stamped status and visible owner would help me hand over unfinished repairs.

turns.speaker: oleg
turns.text: Please do not add payroll or inventory purchasing to the handoff pilot. I have no settled view on manual versus automatic assignment.

turns.speaker: oleg
turns.text: I have not checked the email system's integration options or the rules for storing customer details.

prdBrief: Create a concise product PRD for a two-week, one-shop repair handoff pilot from the selected synthetic interview analysis. Include recurring needs, genuine tensions versus compatible preferences, source-linked prioritized requirements, testable acceptance checks, proposed metrics and a measurement plan, non-goals, unknowns and next steps. Do not turn fictional statements into real customer evidence. Do not decide the disputed assignment policy silently; present a bounded proposed experiment or an explicit owner decision needed. Any numerical success threshold or owner not explicitly supplied is a proposal, not an agreed fact.

reviewCriteria.expected: Synthesizes a shared current-status/single-owner problem using at least Mara, Ivo and Lena or Oleg; does not merely list one quote per person.
Identifies mandatory pre-approval versus automatic assignment without pre-approval for every job as a genuine incompatible policy preference between Mara and Ivo.
Does not call preserving customer email incompatible with reducing manual copying; explicitly recognizes they can coexist.
Does not call a desktop-only pilot incompatible with a shared queue; explicitly recognizes those are different dimensions.
Calls out unmeasured copying baseline, budget or willingness to pay, customer outcomes, integration feasibility/privacy and unmeasured connectivity rather than inventing numbers or consensus.
Keeps scope to a proposed handoff pilot with payroll and purchasing out of scope; preserves one shop/two weeks as scenario evidence, not validated real-world authorization.
Includes observable acceptance checks for exactly one owner, consistent current status, and handling disputed assignment behavior or an explicit unresolved decision.
Defines a baseline measurement and a concrete pilot comparison for copying or stale-status errors; any numeric thresholds, budgets or assigned owners are explicitly proposed.
Key analytical claims and resulting requirements name supporting selected sources or finding IDs that a reviewer can follow; does not cite irrelevant quotes as support.
Clearly labels synthetic evidence and simulation-derived hypotheses, with no real customer claims, population prevalence, invented quotations or externally verified facts.
